utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I call on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Nisha Valabhji appearing on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Valabhji. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Please state your name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Jasna Denona.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I couldn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Should I start over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: In what year were you born?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: On the 22nd of September 1976.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Where were you living in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And prior to that, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: In Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I attended four years of elementary school in Bruska and the remainder of the elementary school in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How old were you in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I was 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about Bruska. Do you know approximately, that is can you give us a rough idea, of the population of Bruska in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: There were about 230 to 240 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Is Marinovici a hamlet which is part of Bruska?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. That's a hamlet in Bruska, a part of Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you recall approximately how many houses comprised this hamlet?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: About eight houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: In terms of ethnicity, how would you characterise Marinovici?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: There were Croats there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what about Bruska?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Four to five homes were inhabited by Serbs. The rest were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How would you describe the relations between the Serb families and the Croat inhabitants of the village?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The relations were proper. They were not hostile in any way, and they did not indicate in any way that something of the sort that happened could in fact happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you, from time to time, in 1991, and prior to December 1991, travel outside your village?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Mostly to Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing soldiers during these trips?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was in that year?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That was in 1991, from September onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall what these soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Olive-drab uniforms of the then JNA army. Some wore camouflage uniforms, without any particular insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to turn to the events of the 21st of December 1991. Where were you on the evening of the 21st of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: In my family home.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Who was there with you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I was there. My mother. Neighbour Jeka, neighbour Soka and neighbour Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your father was not there that evening?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. My father was in Zadar on business, and -- because he was unable to commute to work from Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Why was he unable to do that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That was because bus lines were cut off, interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall why that was, why the bus lines were cut off?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Because of the barricades on the road and because the Serbian side was defending its own state.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Were the neighbours you mentioned, the ones at your house that evening, Serbian or Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I cannot say that because I didn't see them, but based on what they said, I suppose that they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I was actually referring -- going back again to the evening of the 21st of December. You mentioned some neighbours were at your house that evening. I think you mentioned their names, Jeka and Soka and Dragan. Were these neighbours Serbian or Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Soka was a Serb and Dragan and Jeka were Croats. So was my mom.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And what were you doing that evening, you, your mother and the neighbours?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: We chatted about general things, about life in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall what time it was?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: It was about 19.45.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Somebody knocked at the door. I stood up and went to the front door. I asked who it was. A male voice told me that it was the Krajina Police. At first, I thought the voice was familiar, so I asked them again who it was. The answer was again, "the Krajina Police." And then I was already a bit frightened and asked them the third time, in a louder voice, well, tell me who it is, in fact. And then the answer was, "The Krajina Police. Martic's men. Open up." And I could hear a burst of fire outside the door. I went back to the room where we were sitting. I told the party there that I was told that it was the Krajina Police at the door. Neighbour Dragan stood up and went to the front door because he was the only man among us. He probably wanted to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Next, I heard Dragan opening the door, and I heard them ask Dragan, "What are you doing here in Boro's house?" I could conclude then that they knew Dragan because they knew him name and that they knew whose house it was. Boro is my father's name. To that, he responded by saying that we were just chatting, not doing anything in particular. He then asked them whether he could go over to his mother, and let her know that -- probably he thought that he was going to be taken away. That was when my mom persuaded us to try and flee the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you then flee the house?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Where did you run?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: We ran out into the garden and across a wall. When we crossed the wall, I could hear a burst of fire behind me, some four to five metres away. I noticed this because there were lights on, it was night-time, and the second burst of fire hit near my legs and hit me. That was how I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I was hit in my hip and in my arm. I could no longer move. My mother was two to three metres ahead of me. She came back to help me move away behind a wall into a vineyard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How long did you stay behind that wall?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: About two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you ask your companions to get help?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. There were neighbours Jeka and Soka with us behind the wall. The first thing they did was they tied up my arm so that they could stop the bleeding. They used their clothing to do this. When the pain became unbearable, I told Soka to go and fetch her husband, Sveto, because he was the only one there who had a car, in order for him to take me to the doctor's. I could no longer stand the pain. She told me that God knows where Sveto was, and she was afraid of going into the house because of the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Next, neighbour Jeka said that she was going to check what was happening in the house that was closest to us, although there seemed to be some fire, but she was concerned about the fact that one couldn't hear anything. This house belonged to Roko Marinovic, who was killed that very night.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you proceed to go to the house of Roko Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We proceeded to the house, but before that, we heard Jeka shouting and beckoning to us and wailing and giving us different names.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you know why she was shouting, wailing?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Because they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Who was killed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: At the gate to the yard there, she found the dead body of her husband, Petar Marinovic, and that of her neighbour, Petar Draca.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you also see the dead?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Can I just enter a correction? It is not Petar Draca but Sveto Draca. I could see it on the screen before me. In the front yard, there were Roko Marinovic and Dusko Marinovic, his son, dead as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How many were lying dead near that house?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Four people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you then proceed to go into the house of Roko Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. I went in. My mother took the bloody clothes off me, found some bandages, and dressed my wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you encounter anybody in the house?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. Ljilja Marinovic was in the house, the wife of the killed Dusko Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: She told us that her brother-in-law, Ante, was wounded and that he went to Kalanjeva Draga which is a hamlet next to Bruska, that he had gone over there but that she wasn't sure whether he actually managed to reach the hamlet or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Joso Marinovic came. He is the father of Dragan Marinovic, who was killed. He told us that both his son and his wife had been killed. That's how I learned of the death of two more people.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did he tell you how they were killed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did anyone else come to the house later that night?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. After him, Dusan Draca came. He was the father of the killed Sveto Draca. He told us that at the end of our hamlet, there were four people there who were dead, and he could not see their faces because it was night. However, we assumed who these people were and this was in fact confirmed to us the following morning at daybreak.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Who were these people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: They were Krsto Marinovic, his wife Drasa Marinovic, Stana Marinovic, and her mother-in-law, Masa Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you find out how they were killed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The following morning, my mother and our neighbour Kata went over to see them, and told us that they were hit -- they were killed by shots. Their bodies were bullet-riddled.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: As to the dead whom you saw near the house of Roko Marinovic, were you able to see how they were killed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: They were all killed by weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How many people were killed in your hamlet that night?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Of the ten people who were killed, how many were Serbs and how many were Croats?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: One was a Serb, and nine were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Were the victims soldiers or members of any kind of army?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The Croats were not members of any kind of army, and Sveto Draca was a member of the JNA, the then armed forces, but he had the olive-drab uniform and he had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall what his views were on being mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: According to what he said, he didn't want to be mobilised. On a number of occasions he actually refused, but in the end, he was mobilised by force and so presumably there was nothing he could do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you know what he was doing that night?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: He just came to pass the time. He went to play cards, to socialise, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not he was carrying weapons that night?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How would you characterise his relations with the Croat families?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: They were good, friendly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of the others who were killed that night were carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: When you heard the knock at the door that night, did you form an idea as to how many men there were?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: According to my estimate, three, what I could tell behind the closed doors.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How did you arrive at this estimate?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Since there was full moon, I could see the outline of these people through the glass door, and the second person, who was talking to me, was next to the door, to the left of me. And the third person was the one who was shooting, next to the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: As you were running away from your house, did you hear the men say anything else?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. One shouted, "They got away," when they saw us jumping over the wall. And he said, "Uh-oh, they got away. They are fleeing." That's what the -- that's when the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn now to the following day. What happened the following day?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The following day, nobody from the then-authorities visited us at all. We didn't get any medical treatment or assistance. It was only as late as the evening, at around 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What happened at 8.00?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That -- sorry, 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, 6.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What happened at 6.00 the next day in the evening?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The ambulance arrived, and a woman came along with them, and she told me she was from the police in Benkovac. She took a statement from me as to what happened on that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Where did the ambulance take you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: To the medical centre at Benkovac, and then later on the hospital in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: What kind of treatment did you receive?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I was hospitalised in Knin, and I had surgery. And I stayed there for a week, so I was receiving medication and I had had surgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: After that stay of one week in the hospital, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I went to Ljilja Marinovic's parents' because she came to pick up myself and her brother-in-law, Ante, from the hospital at that time, and since she had gone to stay with her parents previously, I mean after those tragic events, we stayed at their place for two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And then where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: And then I returned to Bruska, and I stayed there until the 10th of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How did you feel staying there after everything that had happened?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: It is difficult to put it into words. Terrible. I have no way of telling you, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Let's turn to early 1992, after, I believe, you had -- I withdraw that. What happened after the 10th of January?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I had another surgery scheduled at the Knin hospital because I had a fairly big wound on my arm, and because of the size of the wound, they were unable to stitch it up straight away. So another surgery was scheduled for later. When I arrived in Knin, the hospital was overbooked and they had no extra beds so I couldn't be admitted. So I couldn't stay at the hospital, so I stayed at my former teacher's house, who lives in Knin, and I stayed with her up until the 15th of January. And then I was admitted to hospital on the 15th, so that my arm could be stitched up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And how long was that stay in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I stayed for two days, and I was released from hospital on the 17th of January. And on that day I returned to Bruska once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I have a few more questions on the injuries you sustained on the night of the 21st. After January 1992, did you have to go any further surgery?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. I had another surgery in April 1992, and it was in Zagreb. And then again in 1996, and that was in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: And the last surgery was in 1999 in Rijeka. It was in November 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How is your arm today?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I've got permanent damage and I am -- I've got 50 per cent disability and my right arm is much weaker than my left arm, and it's a bit disfigured.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you at some point return to your family home in Bruska?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: You mean after those events or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. After 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: In what state did you find your family home?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The house had been ransacked, destroyed, and some ammunition had been stored in those houses. It must have been used as a kind of warehouse during the times that we were not there, since we had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you hear of killings in other villages in this area, in the area?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How did you hear of this?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Through the media, on television and in daily papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall which villages these were?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Skabrnja, Nadin, Ervanik [phoen], Medvidja.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How would you characterise these villages, in terms of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Skabrnja was entirely Croat. Nadin was a mixed village and Medvidja was the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall when approximately you heard this in the media?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Skabrnja happened in November 1991. Nadin at around the same time, and Medvidja in either January or February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Going back to the period after the killings took place in Bruska, do you recall whether these killings were reported in the media at the time?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: How did -- did you see reports in the media yourself or did you hear about it some other way? How did you -- how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: As to the Croatian television, I didn't see it myself, but I was told about it when I got to Zadar. I was told that that had been reported on Croat television, because in Bruska we were unable to watch Croat television at the time, and dailies in Knin reported on those events. There were short articles about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Were you interviewed about what took place in Bruska after it happened?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: First of all, as I've already mentioned, there was this female police officer. I don't know her name because she didn't actually introduce herself. And later on, when I was at the hospital in Knin, a statement was taken by Milan Burza who was a police officer, and representative of the JNA, who didn't introduce himself either.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Any other interviews, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: In 1992, yes, in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall who interviewed you in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: A police officer, but I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: When you were interviewed, did you indicate which unit or army the men belonged to, that is the men who came to your house on the 21st of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. I said in my statement that they said that they were Krajina Militias and that they were Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you -- did you ever hear of an investigation into the killings in your village of Bruska?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of persons being punished for these killings?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. I don't know of anyone having been punished for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now like to show -- or to have displayed a document. It bears B/C/S ERN 02915460. Unfortunately unable to see the monitor display right now. It seems to be doing a self test. Is it on the screen? I seem to be the only one -- oh, there we go. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, I showed you this document in proofing yesterday. Prior to that, had you seen it?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to the end of the document? This is on the one and only page of the B/C/S version, and page 2 of the English version. Are we there? Okay. Could we move it a little so that the name at the bottom can be seen fully? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the name at the end of the document?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the name of Milan Burza.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recall speaking to this individual after the events in question?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this occasion?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: It was mostly when he asked me to tell him about the events and I also met him on one occasion when I went home to my own house. If we go back in time, it was when I returned to Bruska from Ljilja's parents' house and Milan Burza took us from the bus station in Benkovac to Bruska in a police car.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And when you told him about the events, do you recall when that was, when that conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: It was in December. I was at the hospital, and I can't recall the exact day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, please take a moment to read this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could we now scroll back up from top and then to bottom slowly? I know the quality isn't very good unfortunately. I also have a hard copy just in case -- if it's somehow easier to discern on a printed paper instead. Could I have the assistance of the usher in also furnishing a hard copy, just in case it's easier to look at?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Have you finished perusing the document?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, because it's rather illegible, some things are correct and others have been slightly modified.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Okay. What in your view has been modified?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: For example, that Dragan asked who was there when there was a knock on the door. It wasn't true. I asked and I talked to them. And the fact that I couldn't recall what direction the shots came from because of the pain, this is something that I have never, ever said. This sentence has never crossed my lips. And I also said that it was Krajina Militias and Martic's men and I don't know for what reason it hasn't been recorded in this document. And it's a rather concise rendition, if we compare it to the actual account of what happened that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Apart from these points which you have kindly highlighted, is this record generally accurate?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: And I don't know whether this detail that we didn't have electricity for six days or whatever, it was three days, and the rest more or less figures, and I'm not really familiar with these dates. I'm not sure what this date in the top left corner refers to, I don't know. If it is supposed to be the date on which the statement was taken, in that case, it's totally incorrect because it was certainly not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could it have been on the date that is mentioned on the third line under the words, "Official record"? Which I think that date is the 27th of December. Is that more likely?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That's more likely. The 27th might be true but I'm not sure. On the other hand, I'm 100 per cent sure that it was certainly not on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, could you -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Could Mr. Registrar please scroll to the top of the document, in particular the top left-hand corner? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read the first two lines, above the words, "Number and date"? Perhaps I'm not entirely clear in my question. In which case I'll repeat. We are looking at the very top two lines, at the top left-hand corner of the document, very short lines. Could the witness please read those two lines, out loud?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: "SUP Knin and SJB Benkovac."

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: One last question. The author of the document, whom we've talked about already, was he a Croat or a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just look at the tail end of this document, please, the original one, the B/C/S version? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, I am Defence counsel for the accused Martic. According to the Rules, the Defence is entitled to put a few questions to you after the Prosecution has done so and I will put to you some questions which have to do with these events. You said that it was the evening on the 21st of December 1991, and that you were in your home with your mother and two lady neighbours. One of them was Soka a Serb, and the other, a neighbour of yours, was a Croat, Jeka Marinovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And there was Dragan too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since we do understand each other, we have to make a pause between my question and your answer, in order for both to be interpreted and entered into the record. Therefore in addition to you four women, the only male person in the house that night was Dragan Marinovic. How old was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Marinovic is a Croat by ethnicity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you explained that your neighbour, Sofia, Soka, Draca belonged to one of the two Serb families in the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. There were four Serb families or, rather, homes in Bruska. Two houses were in Donja Bruska and two Draca households closer to our home in Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that on the evening, your father was away as were your two sisters and brother, that they were in Zadar attending school, is that true?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that at around 8 p.m., somebody knocked at the door and that when you first asked who it was, you felt the voice was unfamiliar -- was familiar. You heard the voice say, the second time, "The Krajina Police. Open up." Now, when you heard this voice, somebody answering the second time, was it the same voice as the one you heard the first time answering your question?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: All the three times, it was always the same voice answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after giving you the answer the second time, the Krajina Police said, "Open up," and then you heard a burst of fire and that was when you decided to leave the house?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. It was after they said the Krajina Police, the Martic's men, the third time that I heard a burst of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you returned into the kitchen, you said that Dragan Marinovic said that he was going to answer the door, as the only male person in the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes that if the witness did answer the interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that upon opening the door, Dragan Marinovic said, "If you have to take me away, can I at least see my mother first?"

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you gave to the Prosecution and in your answers today, you said that the four of you fled the house - this was your mother's suggestion - that you went into the back garden and across the field behind a wall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether, before Dragan Marinovic stated those words, "If you have to take me away, at least can I see my mother," was there something else that you saw that frightened your mother and you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. It was only their conversation when they asked him, "Dragan, what are you doing in Boro's house?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that to the question, "Dragan what are you doing in Boro's house," he answered he wasn't doing anything special, they were just socialising, was it after that that he said, "If you have to take me away, may I see my mother first?"

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Let me think. Yes, when they asked him, he said, no, we are not doing anything, we are just chatting, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next situation you described during this dramatic evening was that you went behind the house across the field, it was dark, there was moonlight, and then you heard somebody say, "They are going away." And was that when you heard a burst of fire?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. I heard a person shout, "They are going away," and then I heard one burst of fire and the second burst of fire aimed at my legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that when two neighbours of yours went behind the wall that was in front of you, you were running behind them, you and your mother, and then you felt a flash of heat in your legs and you fell down. Was it then that you realised that you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. I could no longer move. That was when I realised that I had been shot.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please break before question and answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Your mother came back to fetch you. She dragged you across the wall where you were -- or rather your wounds were dressed with pieces of clothing?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. They took some of their clothing off and they made a tourniquet in order to stop the bleeding and they covered me up with some clothing because I was cold, and as I was also bleeding, they tried to assuage my situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that you spent about two hours in the cold behind the wall?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the pain became unbearable and you asked Soka Draca to go fetch her husband, who had a car, right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that Soka was too frightened to do that and that Jeka Marinovic went to the house that was closest to you and when she reached the house she started wailing and shouting out names of people: Is it correct that upon hearing her shout, you joined her where Jeka was and then you saw what you described?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: We would have reached the house anyhow. She was just ahead of us, and we were behind because my mother was practically carrying me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the time, it's 10.15, perhaps this would be an appropriate time for a break, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Then we'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Denona, we broke when we were discussing you seeing Jeka going over to Roko Marinovic's house, whereupon she started wailing and shouting out names of people. You said that you and your mother joined her and you saw the dead bodies of the people who had been killed there in the yard of the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that this house belonged to Roko Marinovic and that next to the gate on the ground you saw the dead body of Petar Marinovic and a couple of metres away the body of Sveto Draca. When you entered the front yard you also saw the bodies of Roko Marinovic and his son Dusko Marinovic, who were killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that Sveto Draca, a neighbour of yours, who was a Serb and mobilised into the JNA, that he was wearing an olive-drab uniform of the JNA. I did not understand you clearly. Did he wear that uniform that night or was he generally wearing that uniform?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: He was wearing the uniform that night. He was mobilised by the army and probably had a day off on that particular evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how Sveto Draca came to be at Roko Marinovic's house? What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: He went over there in the evening to pass the time, to wile the time away. He came to see Dusko who he was good friends with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you entered Roko Marinovic's yard and saw the unfortunate people killed, lying on the ground, including Roko Marinovic and his son Dusko Marinovic, you explained that you entered the house and saw Ljilja Marinovic there, the wife of Dusko Marinovic who was killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that as you entered the house, you saw Ljilja coming down the stairs, and she said that she was upstairs when they came and killed the four men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that that evening, Ljilja Marinovic, the wife of Dusko Marinovic who was killed, was upstairs with two children of hers, son Jure, who was one and a half years old, and daughter Sonja, who was over two years old, and with the children of Sveto and Sofia, Soka, Draca, the latter was with you the night when you were shot at.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honours, I'm just wondering, is Mr. Milovancevic referring to the transcript of today's proceedings in this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm putting questions which proceed directly from the text of the statement the witness gave to the OTP. The statement was delivered to you and I want to verify the contents, although the gist of it was confirmed here by the witness today. If necessary, I may cite the pages that I'm quoting for but I just wanted to save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: That's okay. I just wanted to make sure where it was coming from, because my learned colleague mentioned -- said, "You explained and so on." And I wasn't -- I didn't think that that was in today's transcript. I think now my learned colleague has explained where it's coming from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my further questions, I will clearly draw the line to make it clear what I'm quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Denona, you explained that Ljilja Marinovic was taking care not only of her children but of Sofija Marinovic's daughter -- children as well and that she -- these -- she was there with an elderly man who was about 100 years old and he was sleeping at the time - he couldn't hear anything - and the children were Dusko, about 3 years of age, and Sladjana, about four years of age. At least that's what you state in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said in my statement but this person who was 100 years old was not upstairs. He was on the ground floor, and he was asleep in his room. Nobody interfered with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP, and this is something that you reiterated today, that the night that you entered Roko Marinovic's house where you came upon Ljilja Marinovic, is it right that you heard that her -- you also heard that her brother-in-law was wounded that night and went to the neighbouring village of Kalanje?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That's what Ljilja told us when we entered the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the neighbouring village of Kalanje was Serb. Ante Marinovic was transported to the hospital in Knin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. The people from the village drove him over to the Knin hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that as Sveto Draca was killed and there was nobody to drive the car, you had to stay in Roko Marinovic's house where your mother dressed your wounds and that at about midnight, Joso Marinovic came; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that Joso Marinovic was crying, he's the father of Dragan Marinovic who was with you in your home and who was taken away by the people and that he was crying because he found that both his son, Dragan, and his wife had been killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that shortly after Joso Marinovic, Sveto Draca came, who is a Serb neighbour of yours -- or actually, I apologise, his name was Dujan Draca and he's the father of Sveto Draca, who saw his son lying dead in the yard and who said that he had passed by Krsto Marinovic's house where he saw four people dead. You also explained that both the police and the ambulance arrived the following day at about 6.00 in the evening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far Benkovac is from your village of Bruska, roughly?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: About 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You -- we told -- from you today that there was no electricity and that there were no phone lines and it was impossible for you to call for any assistance; the only possible way was for you to be driven away somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. We had not had any electricity since the 19th of December. Therefore, three days earlier, the power was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the evening on the following day, the ambulance arrived together with a lady from the police who took a statement from you and that first you were taken to the health centre in Benkovac and then to the hospital in Knin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you taken from Benkovac to Knin because your -- you were seriously wounded and they were unable to help you because they were not able to perform surgery?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The reason was that I was critically wounded and they feared for my life, and because they were unable to provide adequate medical assistance, they forwarded me on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were taken from the health centre in Benkovac to the hospital in Knin, where you had had surgery that night, that in the hospital you saw Ante Marinovic and that the physicians who were Serbs treated you properly. That's what you stated in your statement for the OTP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the wound to your hip was treated in -- well, because it was an entry-exit wound but that your arm had to receive greater treatment. You also said that the hospital was overbooked and you could not be admitted. What does that mean? Were there many wounded?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: There were quite a few wounded in the hospital, and there were no extra beds, which is why I could not be admitted and hospitalised at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But still, after a couple of days, you did explain that you were admitted to Knin hospital and you were re-operated, and then because of the severity of your injuries you had several other surgeries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th of January I was admitted to hospital and I was operated on and I was not at the surgical ward where I belonged but I actually had to stay at the gynaecology department, at that ward, and then I had several other surgeries afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the police from Benkovac talked to you for the first time when they first came to your house in Bruska on the day following the shooting at around 10 p.m., and then they also talked to you for the first time when you were at Knin hospital and it was done by the inspector Milan Burza from the police station in Benkovac, as well as a member of the military police and you don't know his name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Pardon me for interjecting again, Your Honours, but there is a reference to 10 p.m., the police coming at 10 p.m., and my recollection is that the witness has testified that it was 6 p.m. that the police and ambulance came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's my recollection, too. Mr. Milovancevic, what is your response to that? I thought the witness had indicated that the following day, after the shooting, an ambulance arrived at 6 p.m., in which there was a police woman who took a statement from her. Not at 10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just so as to do away with any misunderstanding that's what the witness said. I'm just going to ask her to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Denona, so as to avoid any misunderstandings in the transcript, I don't suppose -- I don't know whether I've misspoken in putting the question but you did say that the day after your wounding at around 6.00 in the evening, there was the ambulance that arrived from Benkovac, is that true?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. It was 22 hours after my wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps the fact that I mentioned the 22 hours was what led to this misunderstanding. The witness has said that it was 22 hours after her having been wounded and not at 2200 hours. So maybe that was the confusion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Denona, you were submitted the official note from the police station in Benkovac and you have been shown the dates when this was drafted. Was it on the 25th or the 27th of December? And this note was signed by Milan Burza as the authorised official. And you said that something in that statement did not correspond to what you said. But my question is this: Is the gist of your story represented here? Do you remember that conversation? You were at the hospital at the time.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I do remember the interview, as I've mentioned. The date, I don't know to what extent it is important but it is certainly not the 25th of December. That was not when the statement was taken. And I have already mentioned those details which are misrepresented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Denona. So in this official note, next to the date at the top of the page, the 25th of December, there is also the text in the main body of the text where the reference is to the fact that you, the citizen, Marinovic -- no. I think Jasna, daughter of about Boro has been interviewed, you're a student born in 1976, your residence or domicile is Bruska, and then it says the date is 27th of December 1991, in relation to several killings. As to what the discrepancies in dates may mean, we can only assume but you did explain that the later Dragan Marinovic didn't ask those people who knocked on the door who was there but that it was you who did that. But in this official record, there is a statement according to which this unknown person, when asked who they were, said the militia of Krajina and then you heard a burst of shooting and then your mother said, "Let's get out." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what's incorrect, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Dragan did not talk to them. I talked to them. And they didn't say militia or but they said, the third time when I asked the question, they stressed, "Krajina Militias," "Martic's men," and that's when they started shooting. And there upon I went back into the room where we had been sitting all along and then it was only then that Dragan got up and opened the door to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether in your statement to the Prosecution, apart from mentioning Krajina Militias, you also used the term "Martic's men" because there doesn't appear in your statement to the OTP. Do you remember that detail?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This is a detail that will probably stick in my mind for as long as I live. I'm never going to forget it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... little bit, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm not quite sure, when you talk about a statement to the OTP are you talking about this statement that was handed this morning or is it another statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this last couple of phrases referred to this official record. The witness explained about the discrepancies between what she actually said and what is recorded here, and then I asked her later on about her statement to the Prosecution because in the statement that she gave to the Prosecution, and that she signed, the reference is to Krajina Militias. But there is no reference to Martic's men. But it is up to the witness to remember whether she has said it or not. So I'm simply asking her whether she recollects, whether she has any recollection of that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, my question is, I think, very simple. When you refer to the statement that the witness gave to the OTP, are you referring to this statement or are you referring to another statement? I don't want -- I'm not asking you about the questions you're asking. I'm just asking you which statement are you referring to, because I want to follow your line of questioning. Remember that the Bench doesn't have, or at least I don't have, a copy of the statement to the OTP, except for this statement that was admitted into evidence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this official record is not the statement to the OTP. It comes from the police. But my question to the witness was in conjunction with her statement to the OTP on the 2nd and the 3rd of November of the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. So there is a second statement. That's all I wanted to know: Is there another statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Denona, you survived a horrific event and apart from the fact that you were seriously wounded, ten people were killed on that occasion. Have you thought about or have you talked to your friends and relatives about the possible motives for such a horrific act?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The only explanation is because we were Croats. I don't see any other reason. Why would innocent civilians and especially I myself, I was a child basically, I was only 15 years old, why would we be a hindrance to anyone? I don't see any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the perpetrators of this crime? You explained that you only saw the outlines of those men but did you manage to get a good look at them?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the late Dusko Marinovic having had a conflict with a person from the neighbouring village, Medvidja, several years before these events and the nickname of that man was Jaker [phoen] or something? I mean you were only 15 at the time but did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. I have never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard from anyone -- since the investigation was carried out by the Benkovac police, did you hear about the fact that the military police got involved and the Zadar police as well? Did you hear that this crime could have been the result of a simple revenge?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I don't know. Revenge for what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There are some data uncovered in the course of that investigation, which are pointing to possible reasons of this, and that is to say that the late Dusko Marinovic had a fight with a man from the neighbouring village, and that man had his finger cut off on that occasion and that's why he was called Kljaka and that apparently he was the one who led this revenge action. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I know nothing about it and I see no connection that we might possibly have had with anyone wanting to take revenge on somebody else, on one man, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I put this question to you because the information uncovered in the course of the investigation, which has been recorded, point to the fact that those men who came to kill Dusko Marinovic afterwards killed Roko Marinovic and Petar Marinovic and Sveto Draca, who was a Serb, simply because they were in the same house and they wanted to do away with any witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: And why didn't -- did they come to my house, then, which is 50 metres away and why did they shoot at me? And why did they take Dragan from my house? And Krsto's house is at least 150 metres away from Dusko's house. Why did they go there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Denona, I would really like to know what the answer to that question is. A normal person wouldn't do that, but what happened did happen. I'm simply asking you whether you had heard anything about that. But apparently you had not. So I was just going to ask you something else. I think in 1993 you gave a statement to Zadar police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It might have been 1992. You said that in 1995, you went back and you saw the house in a state that you've described. Do you have any information as to whether Croatian police ever tried to shed light on this crime and whether they uncovered any information?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that on that evening, in a situation in which four men from Marinovic family or even nine men in all were killed, one of the threatened Marinovic family went to a Serb village and got help and that you were taken to hospital first at Benkovac and then Knin and that you were fairly treated?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: First of all, as to my injured neighbour, he was a neighbour of mine. Yes, he did go to a Serb village and he was driven to the hospital in Knin. It is also true that the next day, at 6.00 p.m., I was taken to the medical centre in Benkovac and then I was taken to the hospital in Knin, and both I myself and my neighbour were fairly treated at that hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Denona, I have no further questions. I do apologise for the fact that I had to remind you of those unpleasant events. That's the nature of our job and that's the nature of these court proceedings. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Ms. Denona, earlier this morning we talked about your father not being at home on the night of the 21st of December due to bus lines being cut off and this was because of barricades on the road. Any idea who set up these barricades?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The Serb side. The army, the paramilitaries, whoever had the upper hand at the time. But mostly the so-called authorities of Krajina. The buses from what they considered to be Croatia, different territory, were not allowed to drive from Zadar to Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a comment. The colleague from the Prosecution is adding other questions that -- it should be in relation to what was asked in cross-examination. Let's not start all over again because this is a question that had already been put to the witness in the course of the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response to that, Mrs. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I was indeed trying to clarify something which I had not asked previously. Should Your Honours deem that this has caused any prejudice to the Defence, this can perhaps be, I would suggest, rectified, if that very narrow topic -- if they have further questions on that very, very narrow topic, perhaps that would be a manner of remedying any possible prejudice that this new but albeit related question has caused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any suggestion on the remedy, Mr. Milovancevic? It's been suggested that if you do want to ask questions on that point later, you would be given the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need for any additional questions on our part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. It is correct, I think that that topic was not canvassed in cross-examination. And I would imagine that in redirect you are really clarifying issues that became unclear during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I shall be more mindful of that. I just have one other question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Ms. Denona, could you tell us what your maiden name is?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mrs. Denona, I have a few questions to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am mindful of the experiences you've gone through. If what I'm asking you, you don't feel like doing, please feel free to say, "I would rather not do that," okay? Do you have an answer for me? It would be appreciated if you would say it aloud so that it gets recorded. This equipment doesn't record a nod. Okay? Okay. You indicated in your evidence that you were injured on your arm and on the hip. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Are you able to -- or do you mind showing your -- you can't show your arm, not from the clothes you're wearing. Can you describe to the Court the injuries you sustained to your hip?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: These were entry-exit wounds from bullets, both to my hip and my arm. However, my arm was more seriously damaged because both the muscle and the bone were damaged. If you want me to show the arm, I can. And the nerves themselves were damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many bullets -- bullet wounds did you sustain to the arm?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: One entry-exit wound to my forearm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to the hip?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Also one entry-exit wound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Did you say it is your forearm that was injured?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes. My forearm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your upper arm is not injured?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You indicated that you may be prepared to show your forearm. Would you like to do that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: This is where the bullet entered and that's where it got out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Explain where did it come in? Where did the bullet enter?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Here. On this side. And it came out on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness shows an entry wound on the inner side of the forearm, and an exit wound on the exterior side of the forearm. Thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to know more about the barricades that were put up on that day. Can you say who had put up these barricades that made it impossible for your father to commute?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I suppose it was the Serb army who put up the barricades, which were there since September when the bus service from Benkovac to Zadar was interrupted. The barricades consisted of all sorts of logs, boulders, and so on. And there was no more bus service on the Benkovac-Zadar line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the Serb army the same thing as the militia Krajina, Martic's police, or are they two different things?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That's the same militia or police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. In your evidence-in-chief, you indicated that you observed how the people who came to knock at the door were dressed. If I'm not mistaken you said some were wearing a uniform with an insignia and one was wearing a camouflage uniform. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The person knocking at my door, I did not see them and I did not comment on their clothes at all. I said that I had seen camouflage and olive-drab uniforms. This was something I saw when I went over to Benkovac. That was where I would see people dressed in uniforms such as these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you went to Benkovac after you were injured or before you were injured, just in your daily movements?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I would see the uniforms before I was wounded, starting from September onwards. Whenever I needed to go shopping to Benkovac I would see people walking around wearing these uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You also indicated that when you finally came back home to Bruska, your home had been ransacked, destroyed, I think you used those two words, "ransacked, destroyed." I would like you to clarify that for me. Was the home ransacked and was it also destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: It was ransacked and destroyed. That's to say the window frames and the -- were destroyed, the bathroom was entirely destroyed. The power installations and so on and so forth, and that's what I meant when I said destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step. When you say the window frames were destroyed, were they pulled out of the wall? Or were they broken?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The frames were pulled out of the wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what became of the window panes?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: They were taken away. They weren't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And so that the window was just a hole, there was nothing to close the window with?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There were just holes. One couldn't close the window because there was nothing to close it with. The frame on which the window rested wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many windows were destroyed in this manner?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: All the windows that were in the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you referred a few minutes ago to the bathroom. What happened to the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The toilet bowl, the bathtub, the bath sink, all were pulled out and taken away. The tiles were destroyed. There was a washing machine that was also taken away. The glass that we had in the bathroom was also taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What kind of glass was this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The mirror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The mirror, thank you. And you also referred to power installation. Happened to the power installation?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: The switches were all stolen away. Parts of the electric cable were torn so that we had to redo the power installations in the house. Nothing was usable any more. The electricity meter as taken away as well, as was the short-circuit -- the fuse box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Was your furniture still there in the house?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No. The furniture was also taken away. There was nothing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your clothes?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: All was taken away or thrown away. I don't know what happened to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did you stay from the time you were injured up to the time when you came back home and found your home in this condition?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: After I was wounded, on the 18th of January 1992 I went to Zadar. I have been living in Zadar ever since. I go over to my village occasionally, as a guest. I got married in the meantime and I'm living in Zadar now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When was this, when you first came home and found your home having been so ransacked and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: It was sometime in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did your mother stay between the day of the injury in 1991 and 1995, when you people came back?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: She also stayed in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did she stay in the same house with you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Since we were refugees at the time, she was in private accommodation staying with our relatives and I was staying in the reception centre for the displaced persons in a hotel Zadar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In hotel Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In hotel Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, hotel Zagreb in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You indicated in your evidence that Jeka Marinovic shouted names when she got to the home of the neighbour on the day of the shooting, do you remember that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: When she entered the house, she saw those dead people, and as soon as she saw them she started shouting their names and wailing. That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: She was shouting the names of the people she saw there lying dead?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for my refreshment, what names did she shout?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Petar, Sveto, Roko, and Dusko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How did you travel from hospital to Bruska, from hospital in Knin to Bruska when you were discharged from hospital?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I travelled by bus to Ljilja's parents' house where I stayed for two days, as I said, and then from Ljilja's parents' house I travelled by bus to Benkovac and then from Benkovac to Bruska we were taken by Milan Burza, who was a police officer at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he take you in his official -- during his -- during the performance of his official duties or was it just a favour he made you?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Let's say it was a favour, but he was on duty at the time and he probably wanted to do us a service, in view of the state I was in, and in view of the state Ante was in because he was also with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to recall the injuries that Ante had sustained?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: They were entry-exit wounds. He was wounded by five bullets, and the wounds stretched from the groins to the shoulders, that area of the body. All in all, he had five entry-exit wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How is he? Is he completely healed and a strong man working and living? Or what's his condition?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: He seems to be doing well. He can move around. He doesn't appear to suffer. However, I believe that psychologically, he is a destroyed person. I believe that it is not easy to endure something of the sort psychologically. Wounds can heal easily but it is difficult to heal the soul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. But do you know whether he's employed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: No, he's not employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know why he's not employed?

utterances.speaker: JASNA DENONA
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Denona. Are there any questions arising from the questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mrs. Denona. You have finished giving your evidence. You may stand down. You are now excused from further attending court. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mrs. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we actually don't have another witness at this time. Since we are not sitting again until next week Wednesday, we didn't think there was time to bring another witness, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Aren't we supposed to be sitting tomorrow as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Here you're talking until next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Indeed. It was today and tomorrow and resuming next Wednesday. I apologise. However, we didn't schedule another witness immediately following this one, in light of the short period in between now and next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. In that event, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My learned friend from the OTP mentioned Wednesday. Is that the 15th or the 16th? Because I want to clarify this. I'm not sure whether I made a correct note of it. I believe that we were sitting on the 16th and the 17th. I don't know if the 16th is Wednesday or Thursday. Is there some sort of error here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wednesday is the 15th and Thursday is the 16th. According to my diary, we are supposed to sit at quarter past 2 on the 15th, Wednesday, in this courtroom, and then 16th and 17th we are supposed to sit at quarter past 2 in Courtroom I for both days. That's what I have on my diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: I also have the 15th, 16th, and the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was a bit confused with the dates. Thank you for the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. May we please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I hear what you say. That is the prima facie view of the Bench on those issues. I'm not quite sure what response there will be from the Defence but looking at those motions, that was the prima facie view of the Bench, that medical certificates were necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were necessary or were not necessary? I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were necessary. Or still are necessary. Let's put it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, I will certainly, of course, discuss it with Mr. Whiting but we will undertake whatever steps we can. Just to inform you the way those conclusions are reached is that we, of course, our investigators contact all the witnesses that we are expecting to bring to find out their status and their condition. So it's through those contacts between our investigators and the witnesses themselves that we obtain this information. It may be then necessary for them to go for further checkups and I only say this so you know it may take a little bit of time, more than a couple of days to get the certificates. But we'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next point, again for the Prosecution, there is a motion to amend the witness list, motion is dated the 1st of February, and in that motion, it is being requested that one Witness, MM-08, is withdrawn as a live witness. Now, this witness's evidence has already been admitted in terms of 92 bis. The question that arises is: Is this request to withdraw the witness as a live witness, does it mean that that statement of that witness should also be withdrawn or does it still stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it was admitted subject to cross-examination. In those circumstances, we withdraw his evidence entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Entirely?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. That was all I had about -- in terms of housekeeping. Okay. We said we are adjourning to the 15th, Wednesday, the 15th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as far as we are aware, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite clear, Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's at quarter past two, in Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of February, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.03 p.m.,
